summary: This RFC extends SIP with a framework for nodes to subscribe to and receive notifications about events from other nodes. It is deliberately not a general-purpose infrastructure for all kinds of event subscriptions.

eli5.summary: It is like signing up to be told when something happens, such as when a friend is online, instead of asking all the time.

subtitle: How SIP nodes sign up to be told when something changes, with SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY instead of constant polling.

tldr.problem: Many SIP services, such as buddy lists, message waiting indications and automatic callback, need one node to learn when the state of something on another node changes, without asking over and over.
tldr.mechanism: A subscriber sends a SUBSCRIBE request naming an event package. The notifier answers, then sends a NOTIFY request with the current state right away and a new NOTIFY whenever the state changes, until the subscription expires or is terminated.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6665 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3265 and has since been updated by RFC 7621. It is a framework only: it cannot be used directly until an event package defines what is being reported.

today: RFC 6665 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3265, and it has been updated by RFC 7621. It remains a framework: it names no event packages itself, so concrete uses come from other documents.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Event Notification
sections.content:
Some SIP services only work if one node can ask another to report when something happens. The RFC lists automatic callback (based on terminal state), buddy lists (based on user presence), message waiting indications (based on mailbox state changes) and PSTN and Internet Internetworking (PINT) call status.

RFC 6665 gives these services a shared framework. It is deliberately not a general-purpose infrastructure for all kinds of event subscription: the author argues that the general problem is far too complex for a single protocol, and aims for something simple enough for simple features but flexible enough for powerful ones.

The document cannot be used on its own. In the RFC's words it is like an abstract base class: it must be extended by other documents, called event packages, before anything can be subscribed to. It obsoletes RFC 3265, keeping the mechanism backwards compatible while folding in several years of implementation experience.
sections.eli5: It is a way for one phone system to say 'tell me when this changes' instead of checking all day. It is only the rulebook, so each kind of news needs its own add-on.

sections.title: Subscribers, Notifiers and Event Packages
sections.content:
A subscriber is a user agent that receives NOTIFY requests about the state of a resource it cares about, and usually also sends the SUBSCRIBE requests. A notifier is a user agent that generates NOTIFY requests for subscribers and usually also accepts SUBSCRIBE requests. Notifiers always act as user agents when accepting subscriptions and sending notifications, even if the node is otherwise a proxy.

A subscription is a set of application state tied to a SIP dialog. It includes a pointer to the dialog, the event package name and possibly an identification token. An event package is an extra specification that defines the set of state a notifier reports, plus the syntax and semantics needed to convey it. An event template-package is a special package that defines state which can be applied to any other package, including itself.
sections.eli5: The subscriber is the person who asked for updates. The notifier is the one who sends them. An event package says what kind of news is being sent, like weather or sports scores.

sections.title: SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY and Their Header Fields
sections.content:
SUBSCRIBE requests current state and later updates from a remote node. It SHOULD carry an Expires header field giving the subscription duration, and a 200-class response MUST carry one too. The response value MAY be shorter than requested, even zero, but MUST NOT be longer. A SUBSCRIBE with Expires of 0 means unsubscribe. Both SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY are target refresh requests.

An event is identified by the Request URI, the event type and optionally a message body. Subscribers MUST include exactly one Event header field naming the event package, registered with IANA. The optional Accept header field lists the body formats allowed in later NOTIFY requests.

NOTIFY tells the subscriber about state changes. Its Event header field MUST match the SUBSCRIBE, and its body carries either the state or a URI pointing to it. A single NOTIFY never ends a subscription by itself, so one SUBSCRIBE can lead to many NOTIFY requests. Every NOTIFY MUST carry a Subscription-State header field with the value active, pending or terminated.

The RFC also adds the Allow-Events header field, which lists the event packages a user agent can act as a notifier for, and the 489 (Bad Event) response, used when the event package is not understood. Proxies MUST NOT insert Allow-Events.
sections.eli5: SUBSCRIBE is filling in a sign-up form that says what you want to hear about and for how long. NOTIFY is each message that comes back. The Subscription-State label says whether your sign-up is waiting, working or finished.

sections.title: The Life of a Subscription
sections.content:
From the subscriber's side, a subscription starts in init. After sending SUBSCRIBE it waits in notify_wait. Receiving a NOTIFY with state pending or active creates a subscription. Pending means the notifier has the request but lacks the policy information to grant or deny it yet. A subscription ends in terminated when a NOTIFY says so, when Timer N fires, or on certain errors.

The subscriber starts Timer N, set to 64*T1, when it sends a SUBSCRIBE. If no NOTIFY arrives before it expires, the subscriber treats the subscription as failed. Because of forking, several NOTIFY requests may arrive from different destinations, and each starts its own subscription with its own state machine and timers. Subscribers MUST also be prepared for a NOTIFY to arrive before the SUBSCRIBE transaction has completed.

When a notifier ends a subscription it SHOULD include a reason parameter. The RFC defines seven reason codes, shown below, and says that other specifications may define more. An unknown reason code lets the client re-subscribe at any time unless a retry-after parameter says otherwise.
sections.eli5: Your sign-up goes through steps: you ask, you wait for the first message, and then it is waiting or working. It stops when either side ends it, and the stop message says whether to try again.

sections.title: Subscribing, Refreshing, Polling and Failing
sections.content:
When a notifier accepts or refreshes a subscription it MUST send a NOTIFY immediately with the current state, even if the subscription is not yet authorized. If there is no meaningful state yet, the body MAY be empty or neutral. The notifier SHOULD check that it understands the package (otherwise 489), SHOULD apply authentication and authorization, and MUST NOT wait for a user before giving a final response to SUBSCRIBE. It MAY return 423 (Interval Too Brief) with a Min-Expires header field if the requested duration is too short. Authentication of a SUBSCRIBE uses 401, never 407.

To keep a subscription alive, the subscriber sends another SUBSCRIBE on the same dialog before it expires. If a refresh gets 404, 405, 410, 416, 480 to 485, 489, 501 or 604, the subscription is considered terminated; other errors leave it valid. If a subscription is not refreshed in time the notifier removes it, and SHOULD send a terminating NOTIFY with reason=timeout.

A SUBSCRIBE with Expires of 0 both unsubscribes and fetches state, so it doubles as polling. The RFC warns that polling should be used sparingly and SHOULD NOT be used where it would cost more messages than a long-running subscription. If a NOTIFY times out (Timer F), the notifier SHOULD remove the subscription. If the NOTIFY gets one of the error codes listed above, the notifier MUST remove it.

Neither SUBSCRIBE nor NOTIFY can be cancelled. A UAS that receives a matching CANCEL MUST respond to it but otherwise ignore it.
sections.eli5: As soon as you sign up you get a first message with the latest news. You must re-sign up from time to time or you are dropped. Asking for 'zero minutes' is a quick way to ask once without staying signed up.

sections.title: What an Event Package Must Define
sections.content:
RFC 6665 puts a lot of its text into guidance for people writing event packages. Authors should first ask whether SIP is really the right protocol; the RFC says to reconsider for things like network management or engine temperature, and says the mechanism is not meant for events that occur more often than about once per second.

Packages should convey complete, well-defined state rather than just a stream of events. For small state (on the order of 1 KB) it suggests sending the full state on every event. For large state a package may use deltas: the first NOTIFY carries full state, later ones only changes, and a version number in the body MUST increase by exactly one per NOTIFY. If a subscriber sees a gap it ignores the delta and re-sends SUBSCRIBE to get a full snapshot.

Each package has required sections, including its event package name, SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY body types, notifier processing and generation of NOTIFY requests, subscriber processing, how forked requests are handled, a maximum rate of notifications and state aggregation. Template-packages are named by appending a period and the template to the package, so presence.winfo and presence.winfo.winfo are different events and the order matters. Behavior marked SHOULD or MUST in this RFC cannot be weakened by a package.
sections.eli5: Anyone making a new kind of news feed has to fill in a checklist: what it is called, what the messages look like, how often they may be sent, and what to do when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Access control: the notifier's user should control who can subscribe, since events can be private, and the notifier should be able to reject subscribers by identity using standard SIP authentication.

Privacy: simply returning some 400 or 600 class responses to SUBSCRIBE can leak policy. In such cases the notifier SHOULD return 200 OK, and the following NOTIFY MUST look like it could contain valid data, so the subscriber cannot tell whether it was authorized. The RFC points to RFC 2779 as mandating this for presence.

Threats: a single SUBSCRIBE leading to a response and one or more NOTIFY requests is described as a classic setup for a smurf attack amplifier, and subscription state can be used to exhaust resources on a victim. Notifiers SHOULD require authentication, with anti-replay protection against replayed SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY requests. Implementations SHOULD provide integrity protection across several header fields of SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY (including Event, Expires, Subscription-State, Call-ID and CSeq) and bodies. Because state can be sensitive, implementations MAY encrypt it and SHOULD be able to handle encrypted SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY requests.
sections.eli5: Not everyone should be allowed to peek at your news, and bad guys might try to flood someone with fake sign-ups. So the sender checks who is asking and, when it must say no, it avoids giving away the answer.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3265
sections.content:
Appendix B lists the changes from RFC 3265, most tied to bug reports from interoperability testing. The headline changes are these.

  • No implicit subscriptions. Subscriptions may only be created by SUBSCRIBE, though the implicit creation by REFER from RFC 3515 is still permitted for historical reasons.
  • Dialog reuse deprecated. Sharing a dialog between usages proved confusing. Notifiers MUST implement GRUUs from RFC 5627 and use one as their local target, so subscribers can target a specific device. Dialog sharing and the id parameter are kept only for backwards compatibility.
  • 202 removed. Implementations MUST treat an incoming 202 as a 200 and MUST NOT generate it for SUBSCRIBE or NOTIFY.
  • New pieces. The invariant reason code, Timer N with explicit subscriber and notifier state diagrams, a new IANA reason code registry, and a MUST for the expires parameter on active and pending NOTIFY requests.
  • State Agent terminology removed, with no change to the protocol.

It also updates RFC 3261 and RFC 4660.
sections.eli5: This is the list of fixes made after people used the first version for years: remove the confusing parts, add clearer timers and reasons, and drop a message type that did nothing special.

viz.caption: REASON CODES FOR TERMINATED SUBSCRIPTIONS (RFC 6665, SECTION 4.1.3)

items.label: Retry immediately
items.desc: Terminated, but the subscriber SHOULD retry now with a new subscription. Used for migrating subscriptions between nodes.

items.label: Retry later
items.desc: Terminated, but the client SHOULD retry later if the state is still relevant, waiting at least retry-after seconds if given.

items.label: Policy change
items.desc: Terminated due to a change in authorization policy. Clients SHOULD NOT re-subscribe.

items.label: Not refreshed
items.desc: Terminated because it was not refreshed before expiring. Clients MAY re-subscribe immediately. Also used when polling.

items.label: No authorization
items.desc: The notifier could not obtain authorization in time. Wait for retry-after if given, otherwise the client MAY retry immediately.

items.label: Resource gone
items.desc: The monitored resource state no longer exists. Clients SHOULD NOT re-subscribe.

items.label: Never changes
items.desc: The state is guaranteed not to change for the foreseeable future. Clients SHOULD NOT re-subscribe.
